beats.intro: Chapter five. [[sub]]Before valuing a stock, you need to know where and how it trades. This chapter tours the machinery of markets.
beats.functions: The financial system lets strangers contract with each other. [[save]]Savers move money from the present into the future. [[borrow]]Borrowers move money from the future into the present, to fund projects. [[raise]]Companies raise capital by selling securities. [[hedge]]Hedgers trade to reduce risks they would rather not carry. [[exchange]]Others exchange assets they value less for assets they value more. [[info]]And information-motivated traders buy what they think is undervalued, and sell what they think is overvalued, which pushes prices toward fundamental value.
beats.assets: Markets trade five broad kinds of assets. [[sec]]Securities: debt, equity, and pooled investment vehicles such as funds. [[cur]]Currencies. [[con]]Contracts: forwards, futures, swaps and options, whose value depends on an underlying asset. [[com]]Commodities, such as oil and wheat. [[real]]Real assets, such as property and equipment. [[note]]Financial assets are claims. Real assets are the things themselves.
beats.markets: Markets are also classified in pairs. [[a]]Spot markets trade for immediate delivery. Forward and futures markets trade for delivery later. [[b]]Primary markets sell new securities from the issuer. Secondary markets trade securities that already exist. [[c]]Money markets trade debt that matures within a year. Capital markets trade longer debt and equity. [[d]]Traditional markets trade conventional securities. Alternative markets cover assets like real estate, hedge funds and private equity. [[e]]Public markets are open and regulated. Private markets are negotiated directly.
beats.intermediaries: Financial intermediaries connect buyers and sellers. [[broker]]A broker is an agent. It finds a counterparty for a client, and does not trade for itself. [[dealer]]A dealer is a principal. It buys and sells from its own inventory, earning the spread between its bid and ask prices. [[exch]]An exchange provides the marketplace and the rules. [[arb]]Arbitrageurs buy in one market and sell in another to profit from price gaps, which keeps prices consistent. [[more]]Banks, insurers and securitizers go further. They create new instruments, changing the cash flows and risks that investors hold.
beats.short: A long position profits when prices rise. A short position profits when they fall. [[borrow]]To sell short, the trader borrows shares and sells them at fifty. [[fall]]If the price falls to forty, the trader buys the shares back for forty, [[ret]]and returns them to the lender. The profit is ten per share. [[risk]]But if the price rises, losses have no upper limit. Short sellers also post margin, because they have borrowed securities.
beats.leverage: Margin lets an investor buy more than their cash allows. [[buy]]Buy a stock at twenty dollars, putting up forty percent: eight dollars of equity, and twelve dollars borrowed. [[ratio]]The leverage ratio is position value divided by equity: twenty over eight, two point five. [[up]]If the stock rises to twenty five, an unleveraged investor gains twenty five percent. The margin investor gains five dollars on eight: sixty two point five percent. [[down]]If it falls to fifteen, the loss is also two point five times larger. Leverage multiplies gains and losses alike. Interest on the loan is ignored here.
beats.margincall: Brokers protect themselves with a maintenance margin. [[eq]]Equity per share starts at eight, and changes dollar for dollar with the price. [[req]]Suppose the broker requires equity of at least twenty five percent of the price. [[fall]]As the price falls, equity shrinks faster than the price, and the ratio drops. [[call]]At a price of sixteen, equity is four, exactly twenty five percent. Below sixteen, the broker issues a margin call: add equity, or the position is closed.
beats.orders: An order states the instrument, the side, and the quantity. [[book]]Here is a market with bids to buy, and offers to sell. The gap between the best bid and best offer is the spread. [[mkt]]A market order trades immediately, at the best price available. Fast, but you pay the spread. [[lim]]A limit order sets your price. It joins the queue at nineteen ninety five. It may get a better price, but it may never fill. [[stop]]Stop instructions wait until a trigger price is reached. They are often used to limit losses, but they do not guarantee a price.
beats.primary: Primary markets are where securities are first sold. [[uw]]In an underwritten offering, an investment bank buys the whole issue, and resells it to investors. [[best]]In a best-efforts offering, the bank only tries to sell it. [[priv]]A private placement goes to a small group of investors. [[shelf]]A shelf registration lets an issuer register once and sell in pieces later. [[sec]]Afterwards, investors trade among themselves in the secondary market. That liquidity matters. Investors pay more for a security that they can sell easily.
beats.structures: Secondary markets arrange trading in different ways. [[call]]In a call market, orders are collected, and traded together at one price at set times. [[cont]]In a continuous order-driven market, standing limit orders are matched by price, then size, then time. [[quote]]In a quote-driven market, dealers post prices, and investors trade against them. [[broker]]In brokered markets, a broker searches for a counterparty for unique instruments. [[note]]Transparent markets, where prices and quantities are visible, generally have lower trading costs.
beats.quality: What makes a financial system work well? [[comp]]Complete markets: the instruments people need are available. [[liq]]Liquid markets: you can trade when you want, at low cost. [[ops]]Operational efficiency: low costs of trading and raising capital. [[info]]And informational efficiency: prices reflect available information. [[reg]]Regulators aim for fair and orderly markets: prices that reflect fundamental value, without excessive transaction costs.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]The financial system moves money through time, shifts risk, and swaps assets. [[w2]]Brokers act as agents, dealers as principals, and arbitrageurs link markets. [[w3]]Leverage ratio equals position over equity, and it multiplies both gains and losses. [[w4]]Market orders trade fast. Limit orders trade at your price, if they trade at all.
